newsitem.title: GERMANY: INSTANT VIEW - German state CPI data for January.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW - German state CPI data for January.

text.p: Following are reactions to consumer price index data from the German states of Baden-Wuerttemberg and Bavaria, which showed year-on-year rises of 1.7 percent and 1.6 percent respectively.

MATTHIAS HAFFNER, ECONOMIST BZW FRANKFURT: "(Bavarian prices) appeared not to have risen so strongly as in Baden-Wuerttemberg. Particularly among foodstuffs, which have a strong weight in the index, the rise was fairly small. We had no expectation that the Bundesbank was planning a rate cut and this doesn't change that (forecast). We think the Bundesbank will continue to wait and see how the currency situation develops, that is the most important factor at the moment.
HOLGER FAHRINKRUG, SENIOR GERMANY ECONOMIST, UBS GERMANY:

"My initial reaction was one of disappointment. Heating oil prices, foodstuff prices, petrol prices -- all the seasonally-affected factors are responsible for the disappointing figures. However, because they are seasonal factors means that the implications are zero.

"There are no serious implications for monetary policy. The figures are a bit stronger than in the previous year because the seasonal factors were stronger -- there was a bottleneck in the heating oil sector.

"These figures show an exaggerated position, they do not give rise to any long-term inflation worries and I think we will see the figures even out over the next few months, although maybe not quite in February already, and the figures will fall over the year."

ARMIN KAYSER, ECONOMIST, SWISS BANK CORP GERMANY: "This is no great surprise, with the figures containing very strong seasonal effects. There is no indication from these figures of pressure on internal prices. Therefore I think we can expect to see a return to a more normal rate -- a monthly rise of one or two tenths -- in the coming months.
